label: paragraph_title
text: FOOD SHIPS.

label: text
text:
NO NEWS ABOUT THE
S.S. "HOI NAM."

label: text
text: As this edition went to press the owners of the s.s. "Hoi Nam" informed the "China Mail" that no telegram had reached them from Kwong Chow Wan regarding the expected arrival there of the vessel.

label: text
text: LATEST POSITION

label: text
text: They have no access to other intelligence. The position and news gleaned earlier in the day follow:—

label: paragraph_title
text: WHAT NEWS IS GOOD.

label: text
text: Interesting developments have followed, in quick succession, the acts of violence on the Chinese s.s. "Wah Shan" which was bringing treasure, livestock and a general cargo from Kwong Chow Wan to Hongkong.

label: text
text: Seen this morning, a representative of the Sui Lee "Co., owners, told a "China Mail" man that he had received "good news" regarding the "Wah Shan." On learning that the steamer had been taken to Shekki, his master had proceeded to Macao, en route for Chinshan, where negotiations had been opened with agents of the authorities directing the strike. The speaker was not in a position to say whether the cargo would be returned—and he gave the impression that beyond being interested in the safety of the ship, the cargo being, perhaps, more a matter for the shippers and/or consignees—but his information was that there was little anxiety as to the ultimate fate of the "Wah Shan."

label: paragraph_title
text: "Hoi Nam" A Marked Ship!

label: text
text: Yesterday an unconfirmed report was mentioned in the "China Mail," that the s.s. "Hoi Nam," flying in the same trade, had also been menaced by armed Bolshevik vessels.

label: text
text: This morning, the local office of the owners said that they had not been advised accordingly. They recognised the fact that the "Hoi Nam"—although she flew the Portuguese flag—was a marked ship, having incurred the hostility of the Canton Strike. Executive because she had never ceased running since the strike began. For this reason, and because threats had been received warning them against transporting foodstuffs to Hongkong, they had given definite instructions to the Kwong Chow Wan agents to telegraph as soon as the ship arrived there.

label: text
text:
Under normal conditions, it took the "Hoi Nam" thirty hours to make the direct trip from this Colony to the French port. Having left on Wednesday morning, the "Hoi Nam" should have reached port last night but a cable was not due till to-day. When the "Mail" reporter called, such a message had not been received.
In passing, it should be noted that as the "Hoi Nam" was outward bound from Hongkong, she

label: paragraph_title
text: Change of Registry?

label: text
text: As reported in yesterday's issue, the Chinese s.s. "Chung Hing" has returned here from Kwong Chow Wan.. She was due to leave again this morning but her departure has been postponed. A gentleman engaged in the trade said he had been told that the "Chung Hing" was going into dock but he "had it straight from the horse's mouth" that the delay was necessitated by steps to place the vessel under foreign registry!

label: text
text: The same speaker also accused certain small armed boats of the Canton Navy as having joined hands with the strikers in this attack. In his opinion it was only a campaign to exact squeeze. Many a commander in the fleet had cast covetous eyes on Kwong Chow Wan shipping. Had their hulls been sufficiently seaworthy, they would have ventured out long ago, irrespective of the present boycott, embargo or strike.

label: text
text:
Old Offenders Want Squeeze.
So far, the cruiser "Wing Fung" was the only warship big enough to come out into the open. Had the "Wah Shan" not made for Macao and hugged the coast, she might have escaped, he continued. Unless drastic action were taken, there was nothing to prevent this illegal extortion and blackmail even in ordinary times.

text: A number of European boarding house keepers were summoned to appear before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning for failing to give the Captain Superintendent full particulars regarding their boarders as required by the regulations.

label: text
text: For Mrs. Rowe, of Nathan House, Mr. F. Whitehouse pointed out that a register of the boarders was kept and this was shown to the Police, but he admitted his client had failed to render the necessary return. A fine of $10 was imposed.

text: A raid on an opium den at Stone Nullah Lane was described by Senior Revenue Officer G. Watt when five Chinese were charged before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning.

label: text
text: Three of the inmates were Chinese constables who were indulging in a smoke when the officers entered. The equipment of one constable, who should have been on duty at the time, was found hidden under a bed. He was charged with misconduct and fined $25, or one month's hard labour in default. The others were fined $1 each for smoking.

label: text
text: The fourth accused was discharged and the other man was fined $50 for unlawfully keeping an opium divan.

label: paragraph_title
text: “HONAM'S” TRIPS.

label: text
text:
PASSENGERS NOT ALLOWED
TO LAND.

label: text
text: On the three previous trips rampans were allowed to come alongside the ship off Shameen and take the passengers' ashore, but on Thursday afternoon it was seen that the strike pickets had determined to prevent any of the passengers landing in Canton. Sampans were kept back at a distance from the ship and a strict watch was kept by the pickets to carry out their purpose. That the sampan crews had been threatened of the consequences was apparent from the fact that the few that came near the boat. disregarded the appeals of the passengers to take them away. A strike picket on a motor boat was overheard to say that if they wanted to return to Canton they must come by train.

label: text
text: PICKETS' STRONG CORDGN.

label: text
text: A surprise awaited the 700 odd Chinese passengers who travelled to Canton by the fourth trip of the s.s. "Honam" on Wednesday morning.

label: text
text: the ship sailed for feeding 700 deck passengers or for sleeping accommodation, and it was with the greatest difficulty that the ship's officers brought the passengers back to Hongkong yesterday afternoon. The supply of rice and water was limited, and the passengers had to be satisfied with a bowl of rice each.

label: text
text: A few of the passengers jumped overboard in their determination to get ashore and were picked up by the strike pickets, whose launches kept behind the ship for some distance on the way back.

label: text
text: The "Honam" left for Canton again this morning with about 40 Chinese passengers and a few Europeans, among the latter being the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak.

label: paragraph_title
text: STRIKE EPISODE.

label: text
text: CHIVALROUS PICKET AND CORPSE.

label: text
text: HONGKONG WOMAN'S STORY.

label: text
text: That Canton strike agents are openly working in Macao is one of the allegations made by a woman who has just returned to Hongkong from an up-country village.

label: text
text: Taking her children with her, she left Hongkong by ordinary steamer at the beginning of the strike. This week she decided that trouble would break out in Canton and that, after all, Hongkong was the best place. One reason for her thinking that disorder would break out in Canton was the fact that several imposing bridges of boats had been thrown across her part of the Canton River delta—this being one of the Bolshevik preparations to take Honam. These bridges were not taken down after the danger to Honam blew over, but Li Fook-lam's troops still remained in her village and their proximity was threatening.

label: paragraph_title
text: IMMENSE CLEARING HOUSE.

label: text
text: She went by the regular tow-boat to Canton. From Canton she proceeded by other tow-boats to Heungshan, to Shekki and then to Chinshan which is outside the Macao border. Here the strike pickets have established an immense clearing house. People arriving there, to get into Macao, are closely scrutinised and questioned. If it is admitted that Hongkong is the ultimate destination the person is immediately sent back. Those who have the appearance of workers—of either sex—are also frustrated, being detained in large boats until passage is secured.

label: text
text: People wishing to go on to Macao must give an address in that Colony from which a (shop's) chopped guarantee will be forthcoming to the effect that the person concerned is a bona fide resident of Macao. This woman did not know a soul there, but she concocted an address on the spur of the moment. "In vestigators' left that same evening for Macao to look up the place mentioned as all others given by travellers on the same tow-boat. Some of the pickets were, so she told a "China Mail" reporter, chivalrous to the extreme. They pointed out that she had two very young children and that accommodation could not be found for them nor provision made for them. Some wanted to let her go as she did not look like an amah but others were adamant, and she had to pay 14 cents per head for a meal.

label: paragraph_title
text: BOUND WITH ROPES.

label: text
text: Next morning the “investigators” returned. Those who were lucky enough to have had guarantees found for them were released. The address she gave could not be found and she had to stay another day.

label: text
text: Later in the morning she saw a country woman sneak up close to the pickets' headquarters where she turned over a man's corpse to see if it was that of her husband. Four villagers had run the gauntlet in getting vegetables down to Macao that morning. They carried firearms and one striker was killed. The smugglers' casualties were not known. This country woman had turned over the striker's dead body by mistake and she was instantly bound with ropes and imprisoned for being a spy.

label: text
text: The next morning it was decided to let the Hongkong woman go. Her money had been taken from her—she knew not where—and so a sampan was ordered to give her a free passage to Macao, whence she came over to Hongkong.
